title: Teacher freedom - how much, what and when?
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Prompted by US legislation on curriculum, a frustrated reader comment about idiosyncratic teaching and a controversy over a teacher's remarks, Skelton asks how much freedom teachers should have. He starts from the observation that teaching has always balanced freedom and constraint, listing age, curriculum, cultural norms and community views on one side and personality, unobserved classrooms and the right to resign on the other. He then runs a learning-focused school through his definition of learning, seven classroom questions and the factors that affect learning, concluding that such a school both removes and protects freedoms. Teachers lose the freedom to skip repeated experiences, use one method for everything, resist classroom visits or overload students, but keep freedom to improvise, shape curriculum and feed back on school systems. His close is that consistency across a school is the price of better learning, and the balance is a judgement call.
points: Teacher freedom has never been absolute, since age, curriculum, culture and community always constrain what teachers do.
In a learning-focused school teachers give up freedom to ignore repeated experiences, to adopt a single method for all learning, or to block evidence-gathering visits to their rooms.
Teachers keep, and should have, wide freedom to improvise in the moment, like a skier off the manual, as long as learning is appropriate, sufficient and engaging.
Teachers must be free to contribute to curriculum choice and to tell leaders how school systems hinder learning, because leaders otherwise lack crucial evidence.
Consistency across a school improves outcomes, and like orchestras or kitchens it inevitably costs individuals some freedoms.
quotes: Teachers have never had the type of freedom set out in the Merriam-Webster definition. The act and art of teaching has always been a careful (or, at times, not so careful) balance between freedom and constraint.
When teachers are able to operate their classrooms as secret spaces, they can hit children, treat them unmercifully and generally maintain an abusive atmosphere.
In a learning-focused school, teachers shouldn’t have the freedom to let their students be ‘busy but not busy learning.
Neither should they be able to refuse visits to their classrooms by school leaders and others who want to help them develop evidence that learning is happening (or not).

In a learning-focused school, teachers should have considerable freedom (within the overall goal of appropriate, sufficient and engaging learning) to improvise in ways that make sure learning actually happens for as many students as possible.
The inevitable consequence of developing consistency is that teachers have to give up some freedoms which would get in the way of that consistency happening.
